We demonstrate that in these systems,  the average value of a commutator,  which represents the amount of information carried by fluctuations,  must always be non-negative.  This condition is shown to be met through a mathematical verification of the positivity of a specific matrix.  We further analyze this matrix to identify its components and  show that in many common applications,  the positivity of the system is automatically confirmed without the need for additional verification.  However,  we also highlight a fundamental flaw in the traditional Bogoliubov approximation,  which fails to capture certain essential features of the quantum system.  We derive corrected expressions for the matrix components and  demonstrate that these may still be factored into a product of two positive matrices,  but this is no longer guaranteed in its simplest form.  We provide a more general approach for verifying the positivity of the system and  also establish an alternative relationship between the same matrix,  which may be useful in certain applications.  This verification process is shown to be relevant in models involving the interaction of systems with continuous and discrete degrees of freedom,  as well as in models incorporating chemical potentials,  but its validity is compromised when the system's phase space is divided into uneven regions.  We attribute the non-negative value of the average commutator to a quantum dissipation dynamics,  which transports quantum information in time,  but this does not account for the transfer of quantum information between different regions of the system.  We explore the implications of this phenomenon for the measurement of entropy,  which is shown to result from the loss of information due to the collapse of quantum states during the application of a measurement operator to the system. To make object detection more accessible, the task of supervised object box localization has been proposed, where the labels provided include object classes and distorted box coordinates.  Current state-of-the-art methods for object box localization leverage masked object detection models, which first identify objects and then predict the distorted box coordinates.  These models, however, are trained on datasets with well-formed bounding boxes, which hinders their application to datasets with poorly defined or no box labels at all.  To address this issue, we propose a new approach to object box localization that separates the task into two sub-tasks: first identifying objects and then predicting box coordinates for each object, but does so using two entirely independent networks.  We call this approach Two-Stage Object Box Localization (TSOBL), where two networks operate independently, with one responsible for object classification and another for box coordinate prediction, with the latter using a custom distillation technique to leverage the classification network's feature extractor.  We demonstrate that our TSOBL approach specifically the PICONet-TS, which is based on two independent masked object detection networks, can effectively recover the original box labels from the distorted ones, and even improve the robustness of the model, which cannot be achieved by other state-of-the-art methods like PICONet-M and Local-BLEND.  Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called the OpenImages30k-D (OI30k-D) that includes distorted box labels for the open-source dataset OpenImages30k.  On the OI30k-D dataset that contains both well-defined and poorly defined box labels, our proposed PICONet-TS model excels over other state-of-the-art methods by a significant margin. increasing research is being directed towards utilizing GPS signals for indoor applications, given their widespread availability and understanding of outdoor GPS performance.  However, considering the inherent differences between indoor and outdoor environments, utilizing GPS signals solely may not yield satisfactory results.  To enhance accuracy, this research explores the combination of GPS and Wi-Fi signals for indoor localization.  Initially, a comparative study was conducted to assess the performance of different initialization methods.  A novel approach was developed to estimate the initialization time and location, taking into account the characteristics of GPS signals in indoor settings.  Based on this, a Wi-Fi assisted GPS indoor localization method was proposed, leveraging the advantages of both signals.  The proposed method demonstrates improved accuracy and reduced mean square error compared to sole GPS localization, with results verified through real-world experiments.  The implementation advantages and limitations of the proposed method are also discussed.  Furthermore, the associated code has been made publicly accessible to promote the use of this method for indoor localization applications.  The code can be found at https://github.com/MRTanrikut/WiFiAssistedGPS.  The dataset employed in this research is available at https://github.com/MRTanrikut/WiFiAssistedGPS/tree/master/Dataset. * A comparison was conducted to assess the performance of different initialization methods for a window of possible locations. 
* A novel approach was developed to estimate the initialization time and location, taking into account the characteristics of GPS signals in indoor settings, by examining the signal strength and number of available satellites. 
* A Wi-Fi assisted GPS indoor localization method was proposed, leveraging the advantages of both signals, and demonstrated improved accuracy and reduced mean square error compared to sole GPS localization, with results verified through real-world experiments. 
* The proposed method outperformed existing methods, with a mean square error of 1.85m, by combining the benefits of both signals, leveraging the characteristics of GPS signals in indoor settings, and employing a novel approach for location initialization.

, focusing on how changes in distance and price affect consumption, using data from Uber, food delivery, and ride-hailing services. By analyzing the variation in consumption across different neighborhoods in urban areas, we reveal substantial disparities in consumption volumes among neighboring areas, even in areas with high consumption levels. To model these patterns, we developed a statistical method to classify space into regions with similar consumption characteristics, known as "mixture modeling". Applying this method to 500 meters by 500 meters grids in New York City and São Paulo, we identified distinct patterns of consumption, showing that some areas with high consumption levels are surrounded by other areas with lower consumption levels, which we call "islands of intense consumption". Furthermore, we found that prices and consumption levels follow similar patterns. In analyzing the top consumption patterns in both cities, we found that they are characterized by over 50% of users actively engaged, indicating that certain areas exhibit unique appeal to users. Additionally, by estimating the surrounding effect on consumption within a 500 meters radius, we discovered a non-linear relationship where areas with moderate consumption levels are more significantly affected by their surroundings than those with high or low consumption levels. Consequently, this knowledge implies that services aimed at increasing consumption in areas with low consumption levels should consider the surrounding effect and unique characteristics of those areas. Moreover, our results suggest that pricing strategies should also account for the distinct consumption patterns in different geographical areas, which can be obtained through the mentioned mixture modeling technique. Utilizing this modeling, we found that consumption within a one-kilometer radius of previously unvisited locations can be predicted with accuracy, allowing for the identification of "hidden consumption hotspots". Lastly, we found that consumption in areas already visited by a user can be accurately predicted with high precision, indicating a capability to forecast the user's future actions. This methodology is adaptable to other mobile services and can be applied to study consumption patterns in diverse contexts, providing a suitable approach for addressing the spatial aspect of consumption in mobile services. Collaborative filtering, a prevalent technique for personalization, is susceptible to the space-time consumption puzzle, hindering its effectiveness in this scenario. In contrast, our results demonstrate that opinion-based methods, which can produce a more accurate output when combined with external information, are an equally effective alternative for personalizing consumption in this context, as demonstrated in the supplementary materials.

have long been the default model for time-series prediction tasks in various fields, including finance, weather forecasting, and audio generation.  Nonetheless, RNN's inability to handle vast input sequences efficiently has hindered their widespread use, with bedrock problems like memory constraints and slow training times.  This limitation has created a pressing need for alternative architectures that combine the natural expressiveness of RNN with the computational efficiency of sequential processing.  Graph Neural Networks (GNN), with their RNN-inspired design and efficient batch updates, have emerged as a promising substitute, especially for applications where RNN's historical data utilization is less understood.  This study investigates the applicability of GNN in replacing RNN for time-series prediction tasks.  Our findings indicate that GNN, despite their complex training processes, yield inferior performance compared to RNN in most cases.  This disparity is particularly pronounced when the input sequences are shorter or there's significant temporal dependency in the data.  Conversely, GNN consistently demonstrated superior performance in predictions involving longer input sequences with limited temporal dependency.  This research provides a thorough exploration of the theoretical advantages of GNN over RNN, as well as their practical performance in time-series prediction scenarios.  Additionally, it offers a novel distinction between short-range and long-range temporal dependencies, which can be of significant interest to researchers working on applications with diverse data sets.   The paper also explores the impact of varying interim accumulation rates on study design parameters, highlighting the importance of considering this effect in planning multi-center trials that employ central continuous monitoring. 

  The methods presented are particularly relevant for Phase III trials with extended accrual periods, but the issues at hand are equally pressing for Phase II trials with shorter accrual periods.

the continuous Galerkin method's approximated solution to the time-harmonic Maxwell equation in heterogeneous media. Assuming sufficient polynomial degree and number of iterations for the iterative solver, we establish a pointwise lower bound for the measure of the domain from which local incompatibility (or non-trivial solution) implies unique continuation. This bound is expressed in terms of the energy norm, oblique projection, and accessibility measure, influencing the non-trivial solution's behavior. Notably, this analysis reveals the significance of the transmittivity matrix in governing the local incompatibility's unique continuation property. Additionally, this framework yields a condition for the non-trivial solution's decay rate within the inaccessible region. Our results also enable the derivation of a robust, mesh-independent lower bound for the unique continuation measure, although this bound loses the precision gained from the transmittivity matrix. To validate our findings, we provide numerical experiments using a two-dimensional simulation. These simulations demonstrate the impact of varying polynomial degree and iteration counts on the local incompatibility's unique continuation property. Further, we observe that a higher degree or larger iteration count can lead to a larger accessible region, where the non-trivial solution behaves differently. These results suggest that the number of unknowns plays a crucial role in determining the local incompatibility's unique continuation property. Notably, our strategy for establishing these quantitative bounds may be applied to other iterative methods and various time-harmonic PDE models. Nonetheless, the specific results derived in this study are tailored to the continuous Galerkin method for time-harmonic Maxwell equations. Future research directions could explore similar analyses for other discretization methods, such as the discontinuous Galerkin method, as well as extensions to other PDE models, such as time-harmonic Helmholtz, Schr\"{o}dinger, and Duffing equations. Additionally, we aim to investigate faster iterative solvers to further enhance the local incompatibility's unique continuation property. Ultimately, this research has the potential to contribute to the development of control, identification, and inverse problems for Maxwell-type equations by providing a robust understanding of the local incompatibility's unique continuation property. Focusing on pecking as the most fundamental tool-use behavior, this study seeks to understand its underlying neuroscience and associated brain areas.  When comparing tool-use and pecking tasks in rhesus monkeys, researchers found that both activities engage the prefrontal cortex and the parietal cortex. Furthermore, given its widespread presence across human history, reinterpreting pecking as a fundamental form of tool use can provide valuable insights into the human brain's development, functionality, and associated disorders.  From a clinical perspective, identifying the neural networks involved in this fundamental behavior may lead to the development of novel interventions for individuals with impaired motor skills. first-principle simulations of quantum field theories is a complex challenge, primarily due to the extensive number of possible two-body interactions in a gauge theory with multiple fermion flavours. This study introduces a novel, efficient Monte Carlo algorithm that enables simulations of $U(N_c)$ gauge theories with $N_f$ fermion flavours, where three key developments are implemented: 
 (i) A novel, factorised weight expression for the configuration update, 
 (ii) A novel 'fireball' sampling method for selecting intermediate configurations, 
 (iii) A novel 'histogram reweighting' technique for evaluating physical observables. 
 These innovations significantly improve the computational efficiency of the algorithm by a factor of $O(N_c^3)$, reducing the computational cost to a level where simulations of lattice quantum chromodynamics can be performed on the basis of ab initio fermion interactions. This achievement marks a crucial milestone in the goal of accurately determining the quantum chromonucleus scattering cross-section, a key quantity that cannot be readily obtained from experiments. Further research is needed to establish the accuracy of these simulations through comparisons with continuum lattice simulations, specifically for larger fermion flavours where Symanzik scaling may be observed, or in simulations where the fermion flavours are further divided. Additionally, implementing this algorithm for larger gauge and fermion system sizes is an ongoing effort. This research is an extension of the novel gauge-cluster algorithm developed for $Z_N$ gauge theories, combined with the incorporation of fermion weights within the cluster update procedure. This algorithmic framework is a fundamental precursor to the development of the more sophisticated gauge-cluster simulations of quantum chromodynamics. While this study employs $Z_N$ gauge theories as a prototype, the approach can be extended to $U(N_c)$ gauge theories with the incorporation of degenerate gauge configurations within the cluster update procedure. This algorithmic framework is an essential precursor to the development of the more sophisticated gauge-cluster simulations of quantum chromodynamics.

growing interest in utilizing random complex networks as a representation of synthetic genetic circuits in living organisms. These networks can be defined by specifying connections and intersection points between different molecules, which then produce random output signals. Our research focuses on analyzing the uncontrolled variations in time that arise from these random networks, with the goal of identifying network structures that lead to stable output fluctuations. We based our calculations on modeling these variations using stochastic differential equations, and we found that the stability of output fluctuations is heavily dependent on the degree of connectivity between different molecules and the rate at which they interact. Furthermore, we established an analytical framework for predicting the stability of output fluctuations from this information, and we used this to develop design principles for constructing synthetic genetic circuits that operate in a stable manner. Ultimately, our findings provide a foundation for exploring the complex dynamics within living organisms using the tools of applied mathematics. We also propose the concept of a "designable" time, which could be inherently unstable in living organisms but remains stable in random complex networks; this could facilitate the development of novel therapeutic strategies for treating diseases associated with temporal disorder. Additionally, we found that random complex networks offer a simple framework for replicating the complex temporal patterns that arise from multiple interacting components, and we proposed the concept of a "dynamical phase space" for describing these temporal patterns. Furthermore, we identified various random complex networks that are capable of producing the complex temporal patterns associated with the control of E. coli population growth, and we proposed the concept of a "dynamical robustness" for measuring the stability of these temporal patterns with changes to the network structure. We demonstrated the utility of these ideas through the design of a synthetic genetic circuit that operates in a stable manner, and we provided the underlying code for further exploration of these concepts. Ultimately, our research highlights the promise of random complex networks as a robust and versatile platform for exploring the dynamics within living organisms, as well as the potential to develop novel therapeutic strategies for treating diseases associated with temporal disorder. The underlying theory, which is rooted in the application of stochastic differential equations to model these systems, provides a clear set of design principles for constructing synthetic genetic circuits that operate in a stable manner, and it positions us to explore the intricate temporal disorder that arises from multiple interacting components within living organisms, and to develop novel therapeutic strategies for treating diseases associated with temporal disorder. We have also identified distinct cases of beta symmetry that are independent and exhaustive. Our extensive research on beta-symmetric structures has the potential to contribute to ongoing research initiatives in combinatorics, group theory, and universal algebra. \textbf{Main Contributions}

The thesis makes the following key contributions:

1.  Identifies the $k_{\text{threshold}}$ value for random unitary matrices and establishes its relationship with the Quantum Anderson Localization on periodic lattices.

2.  Proposes an efficient Quantum Algorithm for solving systems of linear equations and matrix inversion when the input matrix has a high $k_{\text{threshold}}$ value.

3.  Demonstrates experimental verification of both theoretical models and the proposed algorithm, specifically involving large-scale random matrices with varying $k_{\text{threshold}}$ values.

This limit can be surpassed by upcoming experiments such as the Axion Dark Matter eXperiment (ADMX) when taking into account the anticipated reduction in background interference, allowing for confirmation of previously reported anomalies in silicon detector data or observations of axion-like behavior in vacuum electric fields.  We also outline a novel, high-sensitivity approach for the Dean mark series of axion searches that can surpass the newly established limit, achieving a detection sensitivity of $10^{-10}$ for a one-second half-life axion decay time, and a limit on the axion photon coupling set in relation to other physics theories.  Furthermore, we propose a proposal for a collaborative effort among the axion community titled 'Axion Dark Matter Frontier', which aims to provide a platform for sharing knowledge and resources among researchers to advance the field, and to encourage the development of innovative, existing laboratory infrastructure to contribute to axion research. significantly enhance various aspects of our daily lives, but their development is hinderingly complex due to the need for simultaneous advancements in mechanical engineering, electrical engineering, and software.  Existing automation technologies, despite their sophistication, cannot fully replace human-like dexterity and precise movement requirements for these robots.  As a result, robotic systems struggle to mimic the ease with which humans perform everyday tasks in a domestic setting.  Our research addresses this challenge by equipping a humanoid robot with force and tactile sensors, enabling it to learn from human guidance via constraint-based motion planning and haptic feedback.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by training the robot to perform tasks such as tying shoes and opening household doors with the help of a single demonstration from a human instructor.  The system's efficiency is further highlighted by successful execution of newly inserted objects and variations in door types, showcasing the robot's capacity for adaptive domestic task learning.  The system's code is openly accessible on our repository for future research advancements.  The emergence of lightweight and compact haptic actuators has made haptic learning more feasible, but existing systems are hampered by their inability to handle multiple constraints simultaneously.  Our research overcomes this limitation by developing a haptic learning system capable of processing multiple constraints through the integration of constraint-based motion planning and simulated haptic interactions.  We demonstrate the system's efficacy by training a robotic manipulator to perform tasks such as tying shoes and opening doors using both force and tactile sensors, but the system has a tendency to get stuck in local minima.  To rectify this issue, we developed a new algorithm called Evac that eliminates the need for explicit constraint detection by treating haptic learning as a global optimization problem through evolutionary computation.  We successfully applied Evac to the training of both single- and multi-arm robots, demonstrating the system's efficacy and efficiency.  The release of our code is open to the community for future research.  Multi-human interactions are a crucial aspect of domestic and service robot collaborations but are compromised by a lack of accuracy in existing sensors, leading to false detections and misunderstandings.  Our research addresses this challenge by developing a robust anomaly detection algorithm based on deep learning that significantly improves the precision and dependability of tactile sensors in a variety of scenarios, enabling the reliable integration of human-robot collaborations through the reduction of false positives and improved communication frames.  We demonstrate the system's efficacy by training and testing the algorithm on data from actual human-robot interaction sessions, showcasing the system's capacity for adaptive domestic human-robot collaborations.

The concept of filters, which translates to multi-scale feature extraction in neural networks, is often taken for granted in both academic and industrial communities.  However, no comprehensive study on the fundamental properties of filters exists.  This work aims to investigate the statistical properties of filters, which are fundamental components in image processing and signal processing applications, using both linear and non-linear models.  Our analysis explores the spectral characteristics of filters, including their frequency response,  and examines the statistical properties of the filter output.  Our findings can enhance the design of filters, which have far-reaching implications for various applications including filter-based neural networks.  We also provide code and datasets used in this work for easy replication of our results.  Furthermore, this work provides a framework for analyzing the statistical properties of other operator-based models, which could be applicable to other domains such as audio signal processing.  In the end, this work highlights the significance of examining the underlying mechanics of such models in order to develop innovative techniques that can tackle the intricacies of real-world data.   The first part of the course covered Dirichlet's theorem on rational
  approximations to algebraic numbers, primarily based on the work of
  Siegel, Strassen, and Rhin. We established the latter's result, which
  specifies upper bounds for the size of algebraic integers alpha, where
  an irrational number theta can be expressed as a continued fraction,
  specifically the degree of the minimal polynomial of alpha over Q, the
  absolute value of the norm of alpha, and the quantity 1/heta - 1.
  
  The second part of the course focused on algebraic integers epsilon, which
  satisfy the property |epsilon| = 1, and we reviewed their connection to
  Galois representations, Siegel's theorem on the distribution of algebraic
  integers, and the non-residue theorem for algebraic integers by
  Lagrange. We also touched on the Gowers-Wigman absoluteness conjecture and
  its connection to the topic. 

  The third part of the course covered Nivel's theorem on rational
  approximations to algebraic numbers, specifically the degree of the
  minimal polynomial of an algebraic integer alpha, which is comparable to
  the quantity 1/heta - 1, and the non-arithmetic application to continued
  fractions. 

  The fourth part of the course covered Diophantine approximation via
  analytic and quasi-arithmetic means, specifically the distribution of
  algebraic integers, and the non-residue theorem for algebraic integers
  combined with the theory of continued fractions. 

  I've included solutions to assigned problems from books by J. S. Miller and
  G. L. Miller, and A. Bouchard and J. S. Miller, as well as additional
  problems not present in the assigned readings. 

  The fifth part of the course reviewed algebraically independent numbers,
  specifically the Mahler measure, Branger's theorem, the approximation
  of algebraic numbers by algebraically independent numbers, and Schanuel's
  theorem on algebraically independent numbers

of the solution to a linear second order PDE with a near diagonal operator, where the parabolic operator contains a non-diagonal term representing a weak feedback mechanism from the second to the first equation. This non-diagonal term causes a significant obstacle in applying classical stability analysis techniques, such as the Duality Method or Carleman estimates, which are otherwise potent tools for estimating the solution's decay rate. To overcome this limitation, we employ an innovative strategy, first estimating the solution's decay rate from below using a modified energy function tailored to counter the non-diagonal effect, and then establishing upper bounds on the solution's decay rate via another modified energy function, despite the non-diagonal term's presence. By combining these two approaches, we demonstrate our main result: a precise expression for the solution's decay rate exponent. Notably, the non-diagonal term's strength determines the solution's decay rate, leading to either exponential or polynomial decay depending on the parameter's value. If the parameter is zero, the estimates provide a precise exponent, while negative values indicate a smoother decay rate than in the corresponding boundary value problem. This outcome also considers the impact of a non-flat boundary on the decay rate. Additionally, our results include a precise estimate for the solution's decay rate exponent in both the stable and unstable cases, along with a contrast to the corresponding boundary value problem. This investigation contributes to elucidating the role of a non-diagonal term in the stability analysis of a system of PDEs. To facilitate further research, we make our arguments' techniques publicly available, showcasing the proposed strategy's applicability to other similar systems of PDEs. To validate our theoretical findings, we present numerical solutions obtained via the Method of Lines. To ensure the method's accuracy, we implement a higher order Adams-Bashforth scheme and demonstrate its convergence. This work may find applications in analyzing the stability of models describing population dynamics, electromagnetics, and other multi-component systems. To explore the non-diagonal term's impact further, we propose an open problem related to stable linear operators and estimate the operator's null space dimension. To facilitate further analysis, we also formulate a linear quadratic boundary control problem for a PDE system with a non-diagonal term representing a weak feedback mechanism from the second to the first equation. This system models a common phenomenon in control theory, micromixing, which occurs when a two-component mixture is subjected to flow. To study this system, we first establish a precise expression for the closed loop operator, then investigate its stability properties.

  In our experiment, we observe the nonlinear interaction between gold nanoparticles and femtosecond laser pulses in a micromachined polymer cavity.
  The presence of the polymer facilitates the occurrence of cavity nonlinear oscillations, which are otherwise impeded in air-filled cavities.

  assumption rooted in outdated statistical theories. We contend that modern machine learning
  research has moved towards more advanced active learning methods that involve labeling

  data acquisition. To address the computational intractability of selecting the optimal sample

Various studies have proposed diverse fault tolerance models and corresponding analysis approaches for different blockchain systems. However, these efforts are largely system-specific and there is a clear lack of general theoretical framework to evaluate a blockchain's fault tolerance. In our research, we propose a novel approach to classify and commonize existing fault tolerance models. This approach enables us to establish a theoretical framework for analyzing the fault tolerance of any blockchain system. By constructing an abstract state machine for the sequence of transactions on a blockchain, we can determine its fault tolerance based on the binary decision diagram derived from the machine. Furthermore, we provide an algorithm to derive the binary decision diagram from the abstract state machine and prove that the binary decision diagram-based approach is more efficient in terms of time complexity. Moreover, we demonstrate our method by applying it to a notable blockchain system called HotStuff. Additionally, we explore potential avenues for future research, including the investigation of computational complexities and the potential for approximation algorithms. The source code for our method has been made publicly available. As a key preprocessing step for subsequent analyses, EEG data must be filtered to remove unwanted noise and artifacts.  Currently, a common preprocessing approach for EEG data in research and clinical applications is adaptive filtering, particularly the least mean square (LMS) algorithm.  However, this method has a significant drawback - it requires a reference signal from an individual with known brain activity, which can be difficult to obtain in certain situations.  A new approach has been proposed - a blind adaptive filtering technique based on the recurrent least squares (RLS) method. While current approaches can handle small-scale networks, they fail to scale to the complexity of modern supply chains. To overcome this limitation, we develop a method for representing multi-industry networks using bill of materials graphs, enabling the use of network flow algorithms to track material flows. We further use our approach to investigate the impact of government subsidies on closed-loop production cycles in these networks, with our results suggesting that targeting the most prominent materials in these networks yields the greatest benefits. A first-order Hall effect model is used, assuming that the MHD generator's plasma and the hall effect device's electrodes have uniform properties and that there is no variation in the electric field across the thickness of the device. Due to symmetry, the electric field within the device only changes in the direction perpendicular to both the flow and magnetic field, resulting in an odd function for this variation. Consequently, an electromotive force is generated at the center of the device, leading to an increase in output voltage and, thus, hall effect efficiency. Additionally, an efficiency of 100 percent can be obtained when the flow and magnetic field are correlated. A note is made about the possibility of operating MHD generators in a Hall effect mode using this concept, particularly in applications where high output voltages are desired, such as in the case of MHD pumps. A distinction is drawn between this Hall effect configuration and another known as the 'Hall multiplier', which generates an electromotive force at the edges of the device due to a Hall current at the boundaries, resulting in an efficiency of the hall effect of just over ten percent. A note is also made about recent experimental successes with the Hall multiplier design. Specifically, this framework, which comprises a set of multi-qubit operators that commute with one another, is used to model various quantum processes.  Certain operations that are capable of transforming a code state into another code state are defined as "free" in this framework, based on the requirements that they preserve the average value of all stabilizer operators and cannot create or destroy any correlated states within the code.  Using both a bare-eyed and cat-state representation of topological quantum codes, this framework is applied to investigate resource requirements for executing both single-qubit and multi-qubit operations within these codes.  Furthermore, this study proposes the concept of a "resource state" that can be created within topological quantum codes, such as the Toric code, consisting of a pair of entangled qubits stored in any two-qubit block of the code, and demonstrates that these resource states are highly resistant to decoherence resulting from interactions with a noisy environment.  Consequently, even in situations of significant noise, these resource states can still provide a reliable source of correlation across qubits within the code, thereby significantly reducing the distance that the information must traverse, and thus the associated error probability, when executing operations within the code.  As a result, topological quantum codes possess a distinct advantage as resource states in this framework, making them extremely well-suited for executing quantum operations in both large-scale experimental implementations and theoretical models of quantum computing.  Moreover, this study also proposes the concept of a "resource gap" that is present when the Hamiltonian defined by the stabilizer operators possesses a non-zero energy difference between the code space and the nearest excited state, and demonstrates that both single-qubit and multi-qubit operations within these codes are facilitated by the availability of both energy and non-energy quanta, respectively, in this gap. It refers to the collective emotional state of the community in response to their experiences, consisting of short-term reactions to current events and long-term attitudes and opinions.  It can be viewed as a complex dynamic process influenced by numerous factors, including political decisions, economic conditions, and natural disasters.  As a result, modeling public mood poses significant scientific and engineering challenges.  Additionally, the task of classifying political speech into positive, negative, or neutral categories demonstrates the difficulty of developing an automated system for this purpose.  This thesis presents a set of innovative approaches to addressing this challenge.  Firstly, a new dataset called CMU-RT09S-ENG-3WAY was created to serve as a benchmark for evaluating the proposed methods.  This dataset consists of manually annotated sentiment categories for dialogues expressed by participants in the CMU-RT09S dataset during periods of high and low public mood induced by the 2008-2009 Global Financial Crisis.  Subsequently, the thesis delves into the design of an automated system for classifying this speech into positive, negative, or neutral categories.  This system was tested using the newly created dataset and produced surprising results, indicating that negative speech has the greatest impact on public mood.  Furthermore, a new theory was developed to explain the underlying dynamics of public mood based on this analysis.  Additionally, alternative approaches to classifying speech were proposed and tested with mixed results.  Lastly, the thesis investigates the application of these methods to a larger dataset, yielding a new model for predicting public mood.  This model was verified through empirical analysis and found to conform to the proposed theory.  All the proposed methods have been made available for further use and experimentation.  The underlying physics of microlensing is intricately connected with the 
 properties of a star or the mass distribution of a compact object, as well 
 as the observer's location. To gain insight into this complex phenomenon, 
 we first examine multiple lensing systems comprising two separate objects,

significant progress in AI research over the last few years, becoming remarkably skilled at both generating text and classifying language-based data.  Despite this, research indicates that the connections between these language understanding abilities and the underlying architecture of the model remain poorly understood.  To address this knowledge gap, we employed a neural network-based language model to scan a massive corpus of text for patterns of association, using both the Kullback-Liebler divergence and mutual information as measures of dependence.  Upon analyzing the results, we recognized key features that are heavily connected with the model's semantic properties, including aspects like grammatical constructions and semantic relationships.  Furthermore, we observed that features linked to the model's generative capabilities, such as contextuality and multi-sentence comprehension, are much more difficult to identify.  To investigate this further, we developed a series of neural network-based classifiers that are able to replicate the model's performance in various comprehension tasks.  Interestingly, we found that the model's classification performance was significantly better than its comprehension performance, suggesting that the model is more skilled at using the patterns of association it has learned for classification purposes than for genuinely comprehending the text.  To take this research even further, we invite other researchers to build on our findings and explore the relationships between language understanding, using both comprehension and classification as metrics.  To facilitate this, we have made available a wide-ranging set of comprehension and classification tasks that can be used to assess the abilities of diverse types of language models.  Additionally, we have designed a user-friendly interface that allows users to interactively explore the associations between the features that underpin the model's semantic properties.  To access this interface and the accompanying materials, users can visit our website at https://neural-text.com.  We have also made available a variety of video presentations that provide an overview of the research, including presentations at the 2021 ICLR Workshop on Deep Learning for Natural Language Processing https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8U6DdDqz6Gc, the 2021 NLP Seminar at the University of Waterloo https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5X2Gq4Zz4Gg, and the 2021 AI in Industry Seminar at the University of Toronto https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5X2Gq4Zz4Gg. submmWave (submmWave) technology has the potential to provide high-gain access point (AP) directional communication, especially in dense wireless environments. However, this technology also enables the construction of unnoticeable and unpinnable passive devices, such as cotton-based reflectors and glass-based directors, which can manipulate the frequency and direction of incoming signals. We propose the concept of sybolic large-scale wireless systems that integrate these passive devices and leverage their constructability, persistence, and manipulability. We then examine two scenarios - a single-user setting and a multi-user scenario - to investigate the possibilities of using these devices to enhance performance, potentially leading to the development of unnoticeable and unpinnable communication enablers. We model the constructed passives' properties and assess the achievable gains in the two scenarios, highlighting the potential for significant performance improvements. We also address the non-trivial design challenge of optimizing the passive devices for the highest gain, although a general approach is provided. We believe this work lays the foundation for an innovative research area in wireless communications. Deep learning based approaches have demonstrated the ability to achieve high accuracy on these tasks using large labeled datasets, but such resources are scarce for many applications due to their expense and difficulty to obtain.  In our work, we introduce a novel approach to collect labeled data efficiently by leveraging the expertise of human crowds in a hierarchical manner. The data collected using this platform is referred to as AN-2, along with a subset called AN-2:Sorted, both of which are new additions to the ActivityNet dataset.  The annotations provided with AN-2:Sorted have been analyzed to demonstrate the challenges and crowdsourced annotation costs associated with event detection.  The availability of these datasets is announced with the aim of facilitating further research on activity understanding from videos by providing a more robust dataset with comprehensive and precise annotations. We demonstrate that this violation does not necessarily lead to the destabilization of black holes, as their stability being unaffected. Moreover, we identify the range of negative pressure values within which the exotic matter does not accelerate the collapse of linearly perturbed spherically symmetric dust clouds, and find this range to be determined by the Einstein radius of the cloud. This research investigates the application of underdetermined systems of linear equations to approximate the optimal solution. By utilizing a matrix with columns representing potential solutions, we derive a formulation that yields the optimal solution or a suboptimal one with a specified level of efficiency. This formulation's efficiency is demonstrated to degrade linearly with the number of feasible regions and quadratically with the number of variables in an ideal scenario, although it may behave irregularly in practice. Several strategies for constructing the matrix of columns are also provided, including an algorithm based on an emerging technique in combinatorial optimization. This approach allows for the creation of a matrix that achieves a high level of efficiency, though at a significantly increased computational cost. The effectiveness of our methodology is supported by data from diverse, real-world applications. In one such example, the model derived from an empirical study was used to create a linear programming problem with over 600,000 variables and 100 million constraints, yielding an approximate optimal solution in under 60 seconds. This timely solution was obtained through the utilization of a single processor with 256 GB of RAM. The model's reduced size is particularly noteworthy, as it measures just 13 GB, thereby facilitating more efficient use of both the processor and RAM. The methodology's overall performance is summarized as the product of three key factors: first, the efficiency of the combinatorial optimization algorithm used to select potential solutions; second, the computational time required to perform this optimization; and third, the resulting efficiency of the matrix of columns. The time and efficiency obtained from the matrix, combined with the accuracy of the final suboptimal solution, also play significant roles, though these variables are not quantified here. The algorithm employed to determine the matrix of columns from the set of linear equations represents an emerging technique in combinatorial optimization. By establishing the equivalence between this system and a system comprising spin-polarized Dirac holes, we demonstrated that the physics of the former can be understood through the lens of the latter.  Furthermore, we established that antiferromagnetic and ferromagnetic long-range ordering can arise in the semi-magnetic barriers, and we determined the critical temperatures for these transitions by means of a self-consistent mean-field approach.  Additionally, we identified the emergence of colossal magnetic anisotropy due to the electron gas's interaction with the magnetic barrier, and we observed that this anisotropy is highly sensitive to the temperature and redshifted towards lower temperatures by increasing Heisenberg exchange strength.  Moreover, we demonstrated that a significant magnetic anisotropy can develop before the onset of ferromagnetic transitions in some instances, and we anticipate that this anisotropy may be observable in experiments involving semi-magnetic systems based on Heisenberg materials.  A vast exchange gap forms in the electron gas's low-energy spectrum when the exchange gap in the magnetic barrier is large, and it does so without entering the insulating phase.  This phenomenon may be interpreted as exchange-induced decoupling, and it could provide a foundation for systems with coupled electron gases within semi-magnetic heterostructures.  Lastly, we found that spin-valve-like magnetic transitions can occur in these systems, and these transitions are mediated by the electron gas's interaction with the magnetic barrier's exchange field.  This phenomenon has the potential to be examined through experiments involving a variety of electron gases, and it may be manipulated by varying the filling within the magnetic barrier.  This could be an important development, as it may enable the realization of coupled electron spins within semi-magnetic heterostructures based on Heisenberg materials.  These findings may also have implications for Lanthanide and Actinide based semi-magnetic systems, as they suggest the possibility of exchange-induced decoupling, spin-valve-like transitions, and colossal anisotropy in these materials as well.  These outcomes could be particularly relevant in contexts involving a strong proximity effect, remote-filled subbands, and a dominant antiferromagnetic exchange interaction. incorporate grain boundary effects to interpret the measured data. Our model 
assumes that the bulk material behaves like a dielectric without resistance,

lower temperatures. We also observed that thermal variation of the conductivity 
and permittivity follow a non-linear trend. Moreover, our two-component model 
suggests that the measured dielectric loss can stem from both the grain 
boundary and bulk components. We attributed the observed non-linear 
thermally-induced magnetic phase transition in Gd$_2$Mo$_2$S$_8$ to a 
magnetocaloric effect, which we further analyzed using our measured data. 
Ultimately, we propose that the magnetic phase transition can trigger a 
non-linear change in the grain boundary resistance, which we believe is the

Current research on deep learning speech coding has primarily focused on single-bit quantization, a technique whose optimal performance remains unclear, especially above 10 kbps.  To address this, we developed a novel deep learning speech coding method utilizing multi-bit quantization, which was trained with a batch size of 1024 and multiple hidden layers.  We demonstrated that our proposed method can achieve superior performance (0.45 dB OSS-48 benchmark gain at 10.7 kbps) and outstanding performance (0.07 dB OSS-48 benchmark gain at 23.0 kbps) surpassing previous deep learning speech coding methods.  Additionally, our method was found to be more resilient to batch sizes (0.35 dB OSS-48 gain at 10.7 kbps with a batch size of 128).  We attribute the success of our method to optimized multi-bit quantization layers and a batch-normalization-inspired sub-gaussian distortion function, which were both validated through separate tests.  We also explored ways to further enhance the coder's performance, which yielded coders with minimal additional complexity, achieving 0.03 dB OSS-48 gain at 10.7 kbps and 0.11 dB gain at 23.0 kbps.  These codes will be made publicly available for further research. These structures can withstand external forces through their inherent material properties or, as seen in tissues like tendons and ligaments, exhibit remarkable resistance through mechanisms not yet fully understood.  This phenomenon is often referred to as the'microforce field hypothesis.'  Our research aims to unravel the underlying dynamics powering this hypothetical force field by investigating how diverse microstructures within tissues respond to even minimal external forces, thereby producing a persistent, long-range restoring force. This insight holds significant implications for our understanding of the fundamental mechanics driving the stability and repair of dense biological tissues.  Furthermore, this research also yields novel principles for the design of intelligent, self-healing materials with broad applications in fields such as aerospace, construction, and biomedical engineering.  These materials must be capable of maintaining structural integrity in response to damage caused by high-velocity impacts, fractures, or diseases.  We have developed a range of materials embodying these design principles through the transformation of microstructures within composite materials, demonstrating their effectiveness through experimental and simulation analysis.  These results show that we can replicate the tendons and ligaments' ability to generate long-range restoring forces in damaged states, along with an order of magnitude increase in stiffness compared to healthy states, using this design approach. However, unlike earlier complex systems with highly interconnected elements, the climate system possesses a clear hierarchy of coupled processes, allowing them to be organized into a systematic, multi-scale framework. Through a comprehensive analysis of climate system fluctuations, obtained from instrumental observations, paleoclimatic records, and computer simulations, researchers have uncovered a unified, scalable structure that reflects the climate system's interconnectedness and defines the diverse scales on which it operates – from a few hundred kilometers to the entire planet. This structural framework, representing the average properties of a superposed ensemble of breather solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations, is shown to be intimately connected with the climate system's propensity to generate spatially localized, self-sustaining wave patterns in response to external disturbances. This underlying mechanism is likely responsible for the emergence of the scale-sensitive structure found in the data, and it possesses a degree of robustness, capable of persisting even in systems where some components are loosely coupled and subject to variation in their own right. This concept of a breather-based universal structure holds promise for streamlining the climate system's simulation in computer models, offering a revised approach that prioritizes the discovery of breather solutions across multiple scales and reduces the need for parameter tuning. This breakthrough has far-reaching implications, suggesting that a similar universal structure may be common to other complex systems capable of supporting localized, self-sustaining states. Therefore, this may provide a solution to the long-standing problem of initializing the climate system properly, as its complex, multidisciplinary nature has historically posed significant challenges.

This chapter focuses on estimating the achievable V2G capabilities from a societal perspective, applying a system dynamics approach and incorporating various factors such as vehicle adoption rates, battery capacities, charging/discharging behaviors, and technological improvements. Our theoretical findings indicate that a banded matrix approximation method can effectively tackle the training issues associated with deep and wide networks. This method involves breaking down a neural network into cascaded sub-networks, where each iteration uses the predictions from previous ones as additional features. By applying this method, a wide network can be transformed into a shallow one with a number of features that is the sum of the previous ones. It is proved that the banded structure facilitates optimization, and the approximated weights can be learned through a matrix inversion process. Moreover, a neural tangent network-inspired analysis is provided to demonstrate that the proposed method retains the optimization dynamics identical to that of the underlying deep network. Experimental evaluations confirm that the proposed method yields significant training improvements for Transformers and a certain Deep Wide Network. As the capacity of neural networks continues to scale up, with networks comprising millions of parameters, the challenge of training them has become increasingly pronounced. This issue is particularly pronounced in deep wide networks, which have been shown to achieve state-of-the-art performance in various tasks, including image classification, speech analysis, and translation. However, the deep wide architecture itself poses a significant obstacle, requiring approximately 1 billion parameters to be learned from scratch. Despite the striking results achieved by such networks, the difficulty of training them to a stable equilibrium remains a significant concern. Indeed, our experiments demonstrate that the existing approximation methods fail to tackle this issue, still struggling to converge the optimized solutions to the desired deep wide network. In this work, we take a novel approach to addressing this challenge, leveraging a banded matrix approximation to transform the deep wide network into a shallow one with an accessible parameter structure. Our proposed method breaks down the network into cascaded sub-networks, where each iteration uses the predictions from previous ones as additional features. By applying this method, a wide network can be effectively transformed into a shallow one with a number of features that is the sum of the previous ones. It is proved that the banded structure facilitates optimization, and the approximated weights can be learned through a matrix inversion process. Moreover, a neural tangent network-inspired analysis is provided to demonstrate that the proposed method retains the optimization dynamics identical to that of the underlying deep deep network. By drawing parallels with the classical electron gas, we establish a new relationship between the plasma's electrical conductivity and the magnetic field strength, which leads to a specific relationship between the plasma's viscosity and the magnetic field. Notably, this model demonstrates that magnetic fields significantly increase the plasma's viscosity. Additionally, we derive a new relationship between the plasma's viscosity and the magnetic field, which can also be expressed in terms of the electron scattering cross-section. This model is particularly relevant for understanding the behavior of plasmas in magnetized regions of cool stellar cores, such as in white dwarfs and neutron stars. data is better explained by the individuals responding to the collective's local 
properties than to a global gradient.  Additionally, our analysis suggests that the 
distribution of the collective's velocity can be used to distinguish between different 
collective motion states, with implications for the use of this type of approach in 
studying more complex collective behaviors.  By further varying the model's parameters, 
we demonstrate that the distribution of the collective can also be manipulated to 
mimic other types of collective motion, such as chemotaxis, light attraction, and 
circadian rhythms driven by an external periodic signal.  This capability could be 
utilized to investigate the impact of both local and global interactions on collective 
motion dynamics.  Conversely, in scenarios where the underlying microscale interactions 
are unknown, our approach may help identify the collective's operating modes and 
dynamics by reverse-engineering the parameters based on velocity distributions from 
field observations.  Furthermore, this methodology offers a versatile framework for 
combining multiple collective motion components, which could be employed to study 
real-world instances of collective motion celebrated in wildlife footage.  This may 
happen in the spectacular migrations seen in geese, caribou, and euclidean space,

Our  research focuses on an intriguing aspect: how the doubles strategy of a team relied on an all-or-nothing tactic at the net affects their overall performance in best-of-three and best-of-five set matches.  We based our analysis on data from all major Grand Slam tournaments between 2010 and 2020, looking at how the net-based strategy of a team, which we defined as their net approach percentage (NP), influenced their winning chances in individual points.  We recognized that there are distinct NP profiles, which we termed strategies, each with a natural sweet spot for the net approach percentage.  To account for any potential biases caused by player pairs choosing different strategies based on the significance of the match, we employed a technique called propensity score matching.  Following this, we conducted our analysis both before and after bias adjustment.  The results indicate that, relative to their opponents, the strategy of choosing the all-or-nothing net approach more frequently is associated with a reduced advantage in best-of-three sets matches but exerts a more pronounced advantage in best-of-five sets matches.  The findings also reveal that the all-or-nothing strategy confers a greater advantage in later stages of Grand Slam tournaments.  The results provide novel insights into the intricacies of doubles gameplay.  The data, which comprises 5,637 matches from various Grand Slam tournaments between 2010 and 2020, served as the basis for our analysis.  The research scope encompasses all world's top-100 doubles players during that period.  The all-or-nothing strategy described herein may be applicable to other levels of competitive doubles gameplay.  The analysis highlights the complex interaction between strategy, talent, and match importance, emphasizing the necessity for contextual consideration in sports analytics.  The techniques employed in this study are highly transferable to other domains of sports research.  The framework developed here is an exemplar for creators of sports video games seeking to integrate strategic variability into their products.  The all-or-nothing strategy can be replicated and analyzed across additional categories of tennis data, as well as in other doubles sports such as badminton and golf.  A simulation-based approach is also presented to model the probabilistic outcomes associated with the all-or-nothing strategy.  The methodology developed here is suitable for deployment on computational clusters via Apache Spark.  A demonstration of the strategy's economic implications using agent-based modeling is also provided. Furthermore, the satellite will monitor the global near-Earth space environment around 2000 km above the planet. If the experimental setup is unaffected, scientists can utilize the tungsten samples for up to 5 years of data collection. The satellite features a 3-dimensional magnetic field and a solar wind sail to replicate a solar wind scenario and maintain its position in orbit. Additionally, BISTAR is equipped with 8 on-board cameras and will carry out visual observations of the Earth, meteorites, and cosmic rays in conjunction with other Chinese and international space agencies. The satellite measures 1.2 meters in length, 0.6 meters in width, and 0.6 meters in height and has a total mass of 42 kilograms. It will operate for at least 5 years and be controlled from Beijing, China. The scientific objectives and operational details of the BISTAR satellite are outlined in this report. If successful, the satellite will provide valuable insights into the global near-Earth space environment and lay the groundwork for future large-scale space science missions in China. Furthermore, the satellite will enable researchers to better understand the interactions between the solar wind, magnetospheric particles, and tungsten targets, as well as provide a unique opportunity for high-school and university students to participate in space science research. By leveraging quantum annealing on a 54-qubit device from D-Wave Systems, we successfully optimized the ground state energy of the hydrogen molecule within a Hamiltonian-based quantum model, bypassing the need to convert between quantum circuits and Hamiltonians.  Our findings demonstrate that even though the model Hamiltonian for this experiment is not directly applicable to real-world chemical observations, it is still valuable for analyzing Hamiltonians used in quantum chemistry simulations.  By constructing a Hamiltonian Hamiltonian that mimics the electron-electron and electron-nucleus interactions while avoiding two-body two-electron interactions, we successfully replicated the ground state energy of the hydrogen molecule.  Furthermore, our results show that the two-body two-electron interactions can be avoided by mapping the Hamiltonian to a two-body one-electron equivalent, which indicates that this approach is scalable to larger molecules with more electrons.  By comparing quantum and classical results, we found that our implementation of quantum annealing on this 54-qubit device accurately replicated the optimal energy found by a classical algorithm, and that this quantum optimization can be achieved with resources that are roughly 10,000 times more efficient than the classical algorithm.  Furthermore, our findings indicate that this quantum advantage can be achieved with devices that are available in the near term, which has significant implications for its potential to make a major impact in chemical research.  We also developed a general method for mapping Hamiltonians used in quantum chemistry simulations, which provides a framework for identifying scenarios in which quantum devices like the one used here can be applied successfully.  Finally, we found that the two-body two-electron Hamiltonian for H2 can be replicated accurately with an error of less than 0.1 eV when the electron-electron interaction strength is set to a value of 1.5 or greater, which indicates that this approach is scalable to larger molecules with more electrons. These techniques produce complex optimization problems that are typically solved using numerical methods that are resistant to formal verification and proof-based techniques.  In contrast, we propose using satisfiability (SAT) and Satisfiability Modularity (SMA) to solve energy-efficient scheduling problems in multi-core processors under thermal constraints. Our research creates a batch of highly concurrently usable data structures that can operate across multiple programming paradigms, including C, C++, Haskell, and Python. We demonstrated previously that these data structures can provide superior performance in sequential applications. In this study, we examine the performance benefits of using these concurrently reusable data structures in both sequential and concurrent scenarios, across the mentioned programming paradigms. Our results indicate that our concurrently reusable data structures can significantly enhance performance in both sequential and concurrent contexts, except for one exception where the performance advantage is minimal. Additionally, we found that the performance gain from using these data structures can vary substantially, depending on the specific programming paradigm employed. Overall, our findings support the notion that concurrently reusable data structures can be an invaluable resource for developers, regardless of whether they are working within a sequential or concurrent development framework, and across multiple programming paradigms. Furthermore, our approach can be an effective tool for the development of safe, concurrent algorithms that minimize or rule out operations requiring concurrent access. Moreover, our previously reported strategy for safely integrating mutable threads can be adapted for use with this collection of data structures, resulting in a concurrent collection module that is both efficient and safe, and available for preview under the name 'Parallel.Collections'. 

  The codebase for this research has been made publicly accessible and is ready for use by other developers, incorporating all the concurrently reusable data structures discussed, along with the test suites employed to evaluate their performance. 

  As an added feature, the codebase now includes a graphical user interface for easily comparing the performance of these data structures in both sequential and concurrent contexts, across the mentioned programming paradigms. 

  This GUI is wrapped within an NAnt script that facilitates the automated generation of graphical performance comparison reports, readily viewable in Internet Explorer, for each of the programming languages supported, simply by clicking a single button. 

  Furthermore, the codebase has been modified to incorporate thread-safe queue and stack data structures, along with a simple worker thread runtime, both of which can be found within the 'System.Threading' module of the.NET Framework, following the release of.NET 1.1.

icksen-Lipperheide model, a pair of coupled wave equations that describe the dynamics of an nematic liquid crystal, for which we investigate both spatially localized and periodic state scenarios. Our analysis reveals that the former yields finite-time singularity formation, characterized by a developing gradient blow-up with a rate influenced by the number of dimensions. Conversely, in the latter, we demonstrate that smooth, periodic states are inherently unstable, giving rise to a family of blow-up solutions with distinct frequencies that emerge from them. These results highlight the intricate relationship between the geometry-driven singularity in the localized setting and the frequency-based blow-up in the periodic one. Moreover, our findings also imply the existence of a threshold separating finite-time blow-up and asymptotic stability for certain initial conditions in the one-dimensional case. Additionally, our theory is backed by a plethora of numerical simulations. Notably, the singularity formation in the localized case is seen to be a complex, multi-scale phenomenon involving both high and low-frequency components, which is a marked difference from the pure high-frequency nature observed in the periodic setting. As the singularity approaches, both the energy and the amplitude exhibit dramatic increases, with the solution exhibiting a mesoscopic, wave-like structure in the process. Nevertheless, the mechanism driving blow-up in both the localized and periodic scenarios remains an open question. It is also worth mentioning that our analysis may contribute to a deeper understanding of nonlinear wave systems and their potential singular behavior. It is anticipated that the detailed analysis performed here will facilitate the examination of other, similar wave systems. The results obtained are a result of a combined effort involving both analytical and numerical methods, with the strategy employed to prove blow-up involved both the use of moving spheres and a coarising technique, whereas the task of identifying frequencies relied heavily on the computation of linearized spectrum. The developed models describe the dynamics of an active nematic liquid crystal, a phase characterized by polarized local motion, a phenomenon recently observed and documented. The described processes of blow-up in both the localized and periodic settings may be interpreted as representations of a more general class of phenomenological models, which capture the essential features of blow-up in active nematic systems. It is also worth mentioning that the a priori bounds derived are susceptible to variation based on the specific choice of Ericksen-Lipperheide model being examined. The occurrence of blow-up in the periodic setting may be viewed as an indication of the dispersal of local polarization, leading to an infinite increase in a solution within a finite period of time.

We use high-resolution simulations of streaming instabilities in protoplanetary disks with a characteristic 10 AU inner boundary, where the outer boundary varies between 30 AU to 60 AU. Our findings show that these simulations consistently produce a disc cavity near the central region, regardless of the disk's total mass. When the disk has a relatively low mass (0.001 M$_{\odot}$ to 0.1 M$_{\odot}$) and a massive central object (M0.01 to M$_{\odot}$), it develops a sharp edge at around 20 AU to 30 AU from the star. However, as the disk's mass increases (beyond 1 M$_{\odot}$ for a 0.01 M$_{\odot}$ central object), it forms a more defined and deeper dust cavity, also producing small rocky planetesimals at around 20 AU to 30 AU from the star. These planetesimals could be responsible for generating exoplanetary system variations and explaining the lack of stars with valid Kepler data that have a large number of small planets. method used in various areas, including science, education, and daily life. Despite its importance, programming remains underrepresented in some fields due to ill-informed criticisms and misconceptions. This thesis focuses on addressing these issues by exploring the psychological and educational aspects of learning programming. 

  Part one of the thesis investigates the relationship between programming and cognitive benefits through a theoretical lens grounded in Cognitive Science. It examines the claim that learning programming confers a range of cognitive advantages, including improved problem-solving skills, enhanced critical thinking, and better adaptability in the face of changing technologies. 

  The second part of the thesis shifts its attention to an empirical study of secondary school students in Ireland. It examines their opinions on a range of topics related to programming, including its difficulty, relevance, and overall value. The study found that the vast majority of students found programming at least somewhat useful and enjoyable, with many expressing a desire to continue learning about it. 

  The third part of the thesis reports on another empirical study involving the same Irish secondary school students. It explored the factors influencing their motivation to engage in a voluntary programming project. The study identified several key drivers of their motivation, including personal satisfaction, the opportunity to learn new skills, and the chance to make a positive impact on society. 

  The fourth part of the thesis describes the development of an educational tool designed to support the learning of programming concepts through a visual interface. It delivers a range of features, including interactive examples, detailed feedback, and customizable content, to help students better understand and retain programming principles. 

  The fifth part of the thesis examines the current state of research into the areas of cognitive benefits, student opinions, and program evaluation, with a focus on suggesting potential avenues for future investigations. 

  The sixth and final part of the thesis provides a summary of the key findings from across the thesis, along with some broader reflections on the importance of addressing the criticisms and misconceptions surrounding programming. 

  Apart from the empirical studies, the thesis consists of primarily theoretical content, with the exception of the program specification described in Chapter 5. 

  Overall, the thesis contributes to a deeper understanding of the psychological and educational aspects of learning programming, with implications for the development of more effective teaching methods and software tools.

recent research on the Eulerian and Lagrangian dynamics of fluid flows with singularities, particularly in the context of turbulent dynamics. We will first discuss observations of singularities in turbulent flows, followed by an examination of theories proposing their formation and properties. We will then delve into the measurement and simulation of singularities within turbulent flows, concluding with an exploration of the implications that singularities may have on the development of turbulence. 

  Specifically, we will examine recent research on the Eulerian and Lagrangian dynamics of fluid flows with singularities, discussing in particular the work of Castiglione et al. on Lagrangian dynamics in turbulent flows and the development of a Lagrangian approach to identifying and characterizing singularities within such flows. We will also review recent measurements of singularities within turbulent flows, obtained both through Lagrangian particle tracking and Eulerian analysis of flux and probability density flux. Furthermore, we will discuss theoretical models proposing that singularities may act as random sources within turbulent flows, influencing both the development of turbulence and the transport of material within such flows. We will also provide an overview of the development of a new approach to simulating turbulent flows, based on the concept of a 'landscape of time'. 

  We recognize that research on the topic of singularities within turbulent flows is an active and rapidly evolving field, and as such we do not attempt to provide an exhaustive review of all related research. Rather, we aim to offer a detailed discussion of the recent research most relevant to the specified topics, with the goal of advancing further understanding and investigation of the dynamics of fluid flows with singularities. 

  We also highlight the need for additional research in the field (outlined in the manuscript's conclusion section), particularly with regards to the transport of material within turbulent flows and the development of a more robust approach to simulating such flows. 

  All the figures presented in the manuscript can be found in the supplementary materials, along with a detailed description of the used methodology. 

  We believe that the review presented in the manuscript will be of the greatest interest to researchers working within the fields of fluid dynamics, turbulence, Lagrangian dynamics and nonlinear systems, as well as graduate students studying these subjects. 

  Additionally, we have made the source files for all the tables and figures available on the arXiv, to aid in the reproduction of the results presented in the manuscript.

an important area of research in Computational Biology. This type of 
network is particularly useful for illustrating the evolution of 
characteristics present in multiple species. It incorporates a

ReRooted Networks. Previously, researchers had established algorithms 
for reconstructing Time-Rescaling Networks from data, which could 
subsequently be used to build Phyologeny Networks. However, these 
previous methods were limited to handling three or fewer species. 
This study presents a novel approach for constructing a Phyologeny 
Network from data involving an arbitrary number of species, by first 
building a Time-Rescaling Network for each pair of species, and 
employing a novel method to integrate these individual networks. 
This integrated network then undergoes a process of root identification 
and edge deletion to produce the final Persistent Phyologeny Network. 
This new approach can be applied to an arbitrary number of species. 
Additionally, this study presents a second method for constructing 
Phyologeny Networks from data, by first building a Rooted Tree for 
each species, and subsequently using these trees to build the 
Persistent Phyologeny Network. This study also examines the issues 
related to metric optimization in this context, by establishing 
upper and lower bounds for the number of operations required to 
determine the optimal network for some test species, and further 
providing a sampling tool that can be used to visualize these 
networks. This study also presents results for Persistent Phyologeny 
Networks constructed from actual species data.  Software developed 
as a result of this study has been made available for download. 
This includes both the time-rescaling network reconstruction 
algorithm, as well as the phyologeny network construction method. 
This software has been utilized to provide the results presented 
in this study, and is available online.

the disease, while another set like steel, plastic, and wooden desks exhibit a
moderate to high risk of doing so. These findings are further visually
illustrated through data visualization techniques which also provide additional
insights. Our methodology is flexible and can be adapted to address other
situations and transmission mechanisms, offering a versatile tool for policymakers
and healthcare professionals to assess and prioritize infection control
strategies in their battle against the virus and future pandemic waves.
